Eucalyptus rubiginosa, commonly known as the Candlebark, is a species of medium-sized to tall tree that is endemic to New South Wales and Victoria in Australia. It is also sometimes referred to as the silver-leaved ironbark, rubiginosa meaning rust-colored, and this name refers to the rusty color of the bark after rain.

This tree generally grows up to 40m in height. Its bark is smooth, powdery and white to cream-colored most of the year, while it can also shed in thin, curly flakes to reveal a green or coppery bark underneath. The young branches are usually coated with a powdery white bloom hence given the name "silver-leaved ironbark". 
   
Eucalyptus rubiginosa also goes through various changes in its leaf phases; starting from the juvenile phase where leaves are sessile, opposite for several pairs, elliptical to ovate, bluish-grey to glaucous, and 7-14 cm long. Then the leaves transition into the intermediate phase, they are lanceolate, 7-16 cm long, and finally the adult phase leaves are lanceolate, 10-20 cm long.

Flowers of Eucalyptus rubiginosa are characteristic of eucalyptus, being white to creamy-white composed of numerous stamens. The fruit is a cylindrical to barrel-shaped or urn-shaped capsule. 

E. rubiginosa appears to have a preference for growing near waterways or in moist gullies, on relatively fertile soils. It can survive in regions with a rainfall of 750mm.

The trees are also often home to various birds and mammals. The wood has been utilized in heavy construction, as posts, poles and sleepers. 

Although the tree is endemic to Australia, like many Eucalyptus species, it has been introduced in other parts. Seeds of E. rubiginosa are available where they are used for potential forestry plantation, useful both for timber and also in a diversification context.

It should be noted that Eucalyptus rubiginosa was only recently classified as a distinct species in the 2000s; prior to this, it was often confused or misidentified as another species, Eucalyptus cephalocarpa.
